newsitem.title: USA: Ford-UAW contract talks drag with no strike.
newsitem.headline: Ford-UAW contract talks drag with no strike.

text.p: Contract talks between Ford Motor Co. and the United Auto Workers dragged on without a strike on Sunday as key economic, jobs and subcontracting issues remained unresolved.

Ford's national UAW labor contract, covering 105,000 hourly workers, expired at midnight EDT Saturday (0400 GMT Sunday), but scheduled parts production continued on Sunday at a number of Ford components plants.
Virtually all of Ford's car and truck assembly plants were scheduled to be idle on Sunday, but equipment maintenance work was being performed at all facilities.
If a deal was not reached by Monday morning, there could be more pressure for a work stoppage, because that was when Ford's U.S. plants were to resume full-throttle production, union officials said.

"Hopefully they'll put something together today. People are getting pretty anxious," said John Kimbro, president of UAW Local 737 at Ford's glass plant in Nashville, Tenn. "Nobody really wants to go out on strike."

The Detroit News reported on Sunday that Ford agreed on Saturday to guarantee jobs for at least 85 percent of its UAW workforce over the life of the contract -- more than 89,000 employees. The provision would require Ford to replace thousands of workers expected to retire in the next few years, the newspaper said.

However Ford spokesman Jon Harmon said on Sunday that several of the most important issues in the proposed pact remain unresolved. "I don't know that any of that's sewn up," he said of the News report.
Harmon said the tone of negotiations remained positive, and Ford was optimistic that it could sign a deal without a strike.
A number of the approximately 400 people negotiating the pact left Ford World Headquarters early on Sunday to get a few hours' sleep, returning later in the morning.

Various bargaining committees met continuously since about Saturday morning in a final push to reach a new national labor contract that might also be used as a pattern for contracts with General Motors Corp. and Chrysler Corp.
The UAW, with nearly 400,000 workers at all three companies, extended contracts at GM and Chrysler while it concentrated on Ford.

Early optimism that a Ford pact would be sewn up well before the deadline gave way to the realities of complex bargaining. Harmon said the 1,200-page contract document was subject to hundreds of changes that could be prompted by an agreement on a major provision.
In a second-floor window at Ford's green-glass headquarters building, a hand-written sign read: "UAW - We will strike."

Jerry Klein, president of UAW Local 248 in Kansas City, Mo., said on Saturday night that negotiators were having difficulty reaching agreement on issues related to outsourcing -- or transferring work to outside suppliers.

The UAW wanted the right to strike when it disagreed with the company's decisions to transfer such work, which would give it greater leverage to preserve jobs. It could only strike when its contract expires and over health and safety grievances.
In the last UAW contract negotiations in 1993, also led by Ford, it took a marathon 40-hour bargaining session that lasted nearly 24 hours past the deadline to produce a settlement.
Negotiations between the UAW and the Big Three ran past the contract expiration deadline in each of the past three pacts -- 1987, 1990 and 1993.
